2. In Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 the petitioner, Shafiuddin Ahamed challenged the vires of Rule 5 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 providing for the Council Committee on promotion, Superior Selection Board and the Special Promotion Committee with power to hold examination for appointment by promotion in the Service of the Republic, the vires of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979, the Notification dated 19.8.91 creating Superior Selection Board, the Notification dated 9.10.91 forming a Council Committee constituting of Ministers and State Ministers and the appointments made by the Notification dated 8.2.92. 

 3. It is stated in the application that the petitioner obtained MSc Degree in Geography securing Second Class from the University of Dhaka in the year, 1965, that he appeared at the erstwhile East Pakistan Civil Service (EPCS) Examination in 1968 and stood first in order of merit in the said examination; that on the basis of recommendation of the then East Pakistan Public Service Commission the petitioner was appointed to the East Pakistan Civil Service (Executive) Class-l and posted as Deputy Magistrate and Deputy Collector to which post he joined on 22.11.69; that the petitioner was promoted to the Senior Scale and was appointed as Senior Scale Section Officer vide Notification dated 12.12.79; that subsequently he was promoted to the rank of Deputy Secretary by the Government vide Notification dated 3.1.85; that the 12 persons mentioned in sub-paragraph (f) of paragraph 7 of the application also appeared in the erstwhile EPCS examination in 1968 along with the petitioner and were selected to the EPCS (Executive) Class-1 post and they also joined as Deputy Magistrate and Deputy Collector on 22.11.69 as the petitioner, that 11 out of the 12 above mentioned persons were promoted to Senior Scale on 12.12.79 along with the petitioner and the 12th one was promoted to the Senior Scale on 15.8.81; but subsequently, all the aforesaid 11 persons were promoted to the post of Deputy Secretary on 3.1.85 along with the petitioner and the rest one was promoted to the post of Deputy Secretary on 16.4.90; that 19 persons mentioned in sub-paragraph (g) of paragraph 7 belonged to 1970 batch of erstwhile East Pakistan Civil Service and they joined as Deputy Magistrate and Deputy Collector in October, 1970; that they were promoted to the Senior Scale on 15.8.81; that three persons mentioned in sub-paragraph (h) of paragraph 7 of the application were appointed as Assistant Commissioner in 1977 on the basis of their result of the erstwhile Central Superior Service Examination of Pakistan held in 1970 and they were promoted to the Senior Scale on 2.8.90 and subsequently those persons were promoted to the rank of Deputy Secretary on 3.1.85 along with the petitioner; that the persons mentioned in sub-paragraph(f) of paragraph 7 are junior to the petitioner as per the Bangladesh Civil Service Seniority Rules, 1983 and as per those Seniority Rules and the General Principles of Seniority published in 1970 the petitioner is senior to all the persons mentioned in sub-paragraphs (f)(g) and (h) of paragraph 7; that during 22 years of service the petitioner has been holding various responsible positions of the Government and discharging his duties and responsibilities with utmost honesty, efficiency and devotion; that he was never served with any adverse remark in his entire service career and he got promotion to the Senior Scale and to the post of Deputy Secretary in usual manner on the basis of seniority and merit; that as per Cabinet decision dated 16.9.89 for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary, one has to serve 5(five) years in the Modified National Scale IV or V and in total he\N must serve 15 years in Class-I service including 5 (five) years in Modified National Scale; but one person of sub- paragraph (g) did not serve in the Modified National Scale for five years and the persons mentioned in sub-paragraph (h) of Paragraph 7 did not serve 15 years in Class-I post; that the Constitution of the Republic of Bangladesh has framed a scheme for the Republic to have a public service Cadre and necessary laws regulating the said Cadre and at the same time provide for the principles and yardsticks and methods for determining the inter se seniority amongst the employees of the Republic; that the Public Service Commission has been created under the Constitution for the purpose of conducting tests and examination for the selection of suitable persons in the service of Republic as well as to advise the President in framing Rules relating to service conditions; that it has been made mandatory for the President to consult the Public Service Commission on the matters relating to qualification for recruitment as well as regarding the principles to be followed in making appointment, promotion, transfer and the suitability of candidates for such appointment, promotion and transfer and also matters affecting the terms and conditions of service; that though the Public Service Commission has been exclusively empowered to conduct tests and examination for selection of suitable persons for appointment in the service of the Republic but the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules provided for appointment by promotion to be made on the recommendation of the Council Committee on Promotion, Superior Selection Board or by the Special Promotion Committee by-passing the constitutional institution namely, the Public Service Commission by the Gazette Notification dated 10.10.91 that the Council Committee on Promotion in violation of the terms of reference, Rules and Regulations and also in violation of the provision of Article 140(2) of the Constitution introduced the interview and examination system for promotion for the post of Joint Secretary and illegally introduced marking system alloting 40% for viva voce, 10% for penpicture and 50% for ten years Annual Confidential Reports; that the petitioner along with 384 other officers have been recommended for promotion for the post of Joint Secretary but he was directed to appear before the Council Committee on 14.12.91 for interview for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary and he appeared before the Council Committee on the appointed date and replied to all the questions put to him to the best of his knowledge; that thereafter the order of promotion was issued on 8.2.92 in' which the name of the petitioner was not included. It is further stated that the Council Committee did not conduct any interview for promotion to the post of Additional Secretaries and thereby committed discrimination by not applying the same law even-handedly in violation of the provision of Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution; that the introduction of interview and the marking system is violative of Articles 140(2) of the Constitution and the so-called examination and test has created scope for arbitrary selection; that the petitioner belonging to 1969 batch of erstwhile EPCS was interviewed with the erstwhile EPCS batch of 1970 and 1977 batch of the Civil Service Officers and thereby included his juniors for consideration for promotion along with him in violation of the provision of Article 29 of the Constitution; that the Respondents by the impugned Notification dated 8.2.92 promoted all the officers mentioned in sub-paragraphs (f)(g) and (h) of paragraph 7 to the post of Joint Secretary superseding the petitioner who is senior to the aforesaid persons. It is further stated that the so-called interview system for promotion for the post of Joint Secretary has been introduced with the malafide intention for perpetuating nepotism and favouritism as well as for the purpose of introducing partisanship in the service cadre purporting to politicise the Civil Service Cadre. 

 4. By filing a supplementary affidavit it is further stated that the provisions of the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 are ultra vires to the Constitution inasmuch as no law has been passed by the Parliament which is the pre-condition for making Regulation; that although the petitioner has been personally aggrieved as being not treated in accordance with law and Constitution in the matter of promotion to the post of Joint Secretary but he does not seek any remedy in personam and the remedy sought for by him is for restoration of the constitutional and legal frame within which the promotion of those performing their function in the services of the Republic ought to be considered; that the petitioner was promoted to the post of Deputy Secretary by the order dated 3.1.85 under the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 and the Notifications Annexure-J dated 10.8.91 and Annexure-K dated 10.10.91- have their origin purportedly to paragraph 6 of the Notification dated 17.7.89; that the power under section 4 of the Service (Re-Organizations and Conditions) Act, 1975 do not empower the Government to make provision for Superior Selection Board and Council Committee on Senior Appointment, Promotion and Service Structure, and that the Notification dated 17.7.89 abolishing the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 is also ultra vires of the Constitution as well as section 4 of the Services (Recorganisation and Conditions) Act, 1975. 

 5. The respondent No. 1 namely, Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment filed an affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter alia that the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 is applicable for appointment either by direct recruitment or by promotion to the post of service specified in schedule I of the Rules; that Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 applies to the post of various BCS Cadre; that schedule II of the said Rules contains provision to be followed for appointment to a service; that ex Senior Services Pool posts including posts of Joint Secretaries are not mentioned in schedule II of the Rules as those posts do not belong to any BCS Cadre and those posts of Joint Secretaries do not come under the provisions of BCS Recruitment Rules 1981; that these Rules have been made by the President in exercise of powers conferred by Article 133 of the Constitution after consultation with the Bangladesh Public Service Commission as required under Article 140 of the Constitution; that the Constitution of the Council Committee on Promotion, the Superior Selection Board and Special Promotion Committee is neither arbitrary nor have these Committees been given unguided powers to hold examination for appointment by promotion to the service of the Republic and the powers to hold test and examination were given to enable them to determine merit and Suitability of the officers for promotion; that Regulation 4 of the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulation, 1979 provides that it shall not be necessary to consult the Commission for appointment to a Class I service or post of any officer who is already a member of Class I service and as such the matter concerning the promotion of Deputy Secretary and above who are already in Class-I service does not come within the domain of the Public Service Commission; that the Bangladesh Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 have been made by the President in accordance with powers conferred by Article 140(2) of the Constitution after due consultation with the Bangladesh Public Service Commission; that there has been no arbitrary exercise of powers as all eligible candidates were given equal opportunity and there was no discrimination amongst the candidates; that the promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary is given on the basis of merit and seniority and not on seniority alone and persons mentioned in sub-paragraph (f)(g) and (h) or paragraph 7 of the Writ Petition have not been considered in violation of the practices or Constitutional provisions; that with the repeal of the Senior Services Pool Order, 1979 and abolition of Senior Service Pool Officers (Seniority) Rules, 1982 which were applicable in the case of promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and above the same practices were followed in the case of the promotion referred to by the petitioner on the basis of merit and seniority; that the petitioner was given equal opportunity along with other eligible candidates and was treated equally and he availed the promotion process without raising any objection; but the petitioner was not found fit and, as such, he could not be promoted; that the promotion to the post of Joint Secretary was considered on the basis of merit and seniority and no discrimination was made in this respect; that the petitioner as well as officers mentioned in sub-paragraphs (f)(g) and (h) of paragraph 7 of the Writ Petition were promoted to the rank of Deputy Secretary on the same date by the same Notification and they were all considered along with the petitioner for promotion to the rank of Joint Secretary; that as per guide lines given by the Government and prevailing practices seniority was not only the yardstick for promotion to the post of Joint Secretary but in order to select competent and most suitable officers merits of the officers were considered along with seniority; that for the purpose of consultation with the Public Service Commission the Constitution has provided for making Regulations and such Regulations have been duly made by the President in consultation with the Public Service Commission namely, the Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulation, 1979; according to Regulation 4 of the said Regulations consultation with the Commission in the matter of promotion to the rank of Joint Secretary is not necessary; and the Council Committee took interviews to determine merit and suitability of the Officers for promotion to the rank of Joint Secretary on the basis of the guidelines given by the Government and prevailing practices in this regard; that there has been no by-passing of the Public Service Commission; that the Cabinet formed Council Committee on senior Appointment, Promotion and Service Structure to deal with the specific function of the Government and, as such, the Council Committee is an authority duly constituted and it is neither illegal nor unlawful nor it assumed the power and function of the Public Service Commission; that the Council Committee itself introduced interview and examination system for promotion to the post of Joint Secretary; and introduced system of allocating 40% mark for viva-voce, 10% for pen picture and 50% for 10 years ACR as per Government guidelines in this respect; that the Superior Selection Board did not recommend the petitioner for promotion; that the Council Committee was constituted with the authority to recommend the case of promotion; that the function of the Superior Selection Board was restricted to submission of eligible cases before the Council Committee only; that different system and criteria have been followed for promotion of officers to different level of posts for promotion of the cadre posts the provision of the Rule 5 of BCS Recruitment Rules is folic-wed, for the promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary, Joint Secretary interviews are taken as per Government decision, for promotion to higher post i.e. to the post of Additional Secretary and Secretary the candidates are selected by the Council Committee considering their merit on the basis of their ACR and performance; as such, there is no discrimination nor any violation of the Constitutional guarantees as provided under Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution; that there was no violation of Article 140(2) of the Constitution; that all eligible officers were duly considered; that there has been no violation of the petitioner's fundamental right as the case of all eligible candidates including the petitioner and his seniors as well as juniors were considered and the petitioner was treated equally and subjected to the same yardstick along with other officers; that interview system was followed with a bonafide purpose to assess the suitability and competence of the officers; that it is not necessary to consult the Public Service Commission in matters of promotion to the post of Joint Secretary and such other posts, vide Regulation 4(a) and 8 of the Regulations; that the petitioner himself availed the process of the interview and as he was not found fit he was not promoted; that the Council Committee took interviews many times previously also as per guideline of such promotions and prevailing practices; that it is denied that the Superior Selection Board and the Council Committee have been formed to be used as a vehicle to promote sycophants and henchmen of the ruling party; that the petitioner cannot claim any remedy under the Writ jurisdiction as he has a remedy before the Administrative Tribunal created under Act VII of 1981. By a supplementary affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 1 it was further stated that the Council Committee took interviews on the basis of guideline given by the Govt.; that interview and marking system was followed by the Council Committee in accordance with the guidelines and prevailing practices in order to assess the suitability of officer for promotion to the rank of Joint Secretary; that the Ministry of Establishment prepared a summary dated 3.11.91 containing the guidelines for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and Joint Secretary which were approved by the Cabinet as well as by the Prime Minister as the head of the Cabinet. 

 6. The petitioner filed an affidavit-In-reply to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 1 and reiterated the statements made in the application and it is further stated therein that the subject matter of the case is very much under the Constitutional jurisdiction of this Court and does not relate to the Administrative Tribunal created under Act VII of 1981; that in terms of Regulations 4(a) of the Public Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations 1979 consultation with the commission is necessary in matters of promotion to the post of Joint Secretary; that the Council Committee took interview for promotion to the posts of Joint Secretary but nowhere in paragraph 1 (C)(2) of the Senior Service Pool Order, 1979 or Rule 5 of BCS Recruitment Rules, 1981 the terms of reference of the Council Committee constituted on 9.10.91 was to conduct test, interview or examinations awarding marking system, rather the Notifications dated 2.4.91, 12.3.91 and 19.8.91 clearly state that promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and above is to be made on the basis of ACR and Service record and that no test or examination would be taken; that the Council Committee acted beyond the terms of reference and interview system was introduced with malafide motive for perpetuating nepotism and favouritism and for introducing partisanship in the Civil Service; that there has been gross violation of the petitioner's fundamental right as guaranteed under Articles 27, 29 and 31 of the Constitution. It is further stated that the Government usurped the powers and functions of the Public Service Commission violating the mandatory provisions of the Constitution in making promotions to the posts of Joint Secretaries. By a Supplementary affidavit-in-reply the petitioner further stated that Regulation 4 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations, 1979 is ultra vires of the Constitution as no law has been passed by the Parliament which, is precondition for making Regulation; that by making Regulation the Executive Authority has pre-empted the law and exceeded the jurisdiction which is not available under the Constitution. 

 8. It is stated in the application that the petitioner obtained M.Com Decree from the University of Rajshahi in the year 1972 and he appeared at the Special Superior Service competitive examination in 1972; that having qualified in the said examination the petitioner was appointed in the service of the Republic as a Class I Officer and was placed in the Industrial Management Cadre service on probation by the Memo dated 22.10.73; that after abolition of the Industrial Management Service Cadre the petitioner was absorbed in the BCS (Administration) Cadre as Asstt. Commissioner under notification dated 4.12.82; that the petitioner was promoted to the Senior Scale on 28.12.85; that the petitioner completed various job training programmes and also training abroad and passed departmental examination; that during his service the petitioner held responsible posts in three Jute Mills and also served as Administrative Officer in the department of Industry; that he also worked as Assistant Commissioner and Upazila Nirbahi Officer and also as Additional Deputy Commissioner; that an official gradation list was prepared by the respondent No.1 on the basis of inter se seniority in which the petitioner's name appeared at serial No. 354 and 127 officers mentioned in sub-paragraph (I) of paragraph 7 who are junior to the petitioner had been promoted to the post of Deputy Secretary on the recommendation of the Committee headed by the Minister of State, Ministry of Establishment vide notification dated 8.2.92; that in the name of the holding of examinations and interviews there were wide-spread abuse of the said tests or examinations giving rise to nepotism and corruption and a committee was set up which suggested review and revision Of the system of maintenance of service record of the Civil Officers; that the said Committee submitted a report in July, 1982 suggesting reformulation of Annual Confidential Report which could help evaluate the merit of the Gazetted Officers; that this new system brought important changes for finding fitness and eligibility for promotions exclusively on the basis of ACR; that accordingly the Bangladesh Civil Service Rules, 1981 was amended in 1985 and the provision for conducting tests and examinations was removed vide notification dated 23.3.85; that although the provision for holding and conducting tests and examination were made and a new scientific system of evaluation was introduced but the Government in power in order to get their own party influence and their henchmen promoted, they introduced not only the illegal committee but also reintroduced the process of conducting examination; that in the system of examination, the respondents introduced an illegal system of allocating 60% marks for written examination and 40% marks for oral examination; that there had been serious allegation about this new system of promotion through tests and examinations by ignoring the recommendation of the Superior Selection Board; that due to the introduction of test and examination the petitioner has been highly aggrieved inasmuch as he has been superseded by officers junior to him; that the petitioner has been discriminated as having been dubbed as 1973 batch of Civil Service being supporters of the Awami League; that it has been possible only to promote 32% of the 1973 batch whereas 95% of 1979 batch who have been attributed as the supporters of BNP, were promoted; that the petitioner being senior to the persons mentioned above he has been superseded by the impugned order on the basis of unauthorized interview and marks system. It is further stated that the Public Service Commission has been created by the Constitution with the spirit of keeping all appointments, promotions and examinations of the services of the Republic above any bias, prejudice and discrimination and with this end in view the gentlemen who constituted in the said Commission have to subscribe oath under Article 148 of the Constitution; that the respondents usurping the powers and functions of the Public Service Commission with the malafide motive have formed the Superior Selection Board and Council Committee with a view to promoting sycophants of the ruling party to the posts of Deputy Secretaries and to create a cadre of political loyalists in the service of the Republic. 

 9. The respondent No. 1 filed an affidavit-in-opposition wherein it has been stated that the notification dated 4.12.91 constituting a Committee for the purpose of making appointment by promotion to the posts of Deputy Secretaries was issued with due approval of the competent authority as per the existing rules and regulations; that these rules have been made by the President in exercise of the powers confered under Article 133 of the Constitution after due consultation with the Public Service Commission as required under Article 140 of the Constitution; that the constitution of the Council Committee on Promotion, the Superior Selection Board and Special Promotion Committee is neither arbitrary nor have those committees been given unguided powers to hold tests and examination nor appointment by promotions to the service of the Republic; that the powers to hold interview were given to enable them to determine the merit and suitability of the officers for promotion; that Regulation 4 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultations) Regulations, 1979 provides that it shall not be necessary for consultation with the Commission for appointment to a Class-I Service or post of any officer who is already a member of Class I, or holding a Class I post and, as such, the promotion to the Deputy Secretaries who were already in Class I Service does not come within the domain of the Commission; That Rule 5 of the BCS Recruitment Rules is not ultra vires of the Constitution; that the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultations) Regulations, 1979 have been made by the President in accordance with the powers conferred by Articles 133 of the Constitution after due consultation with the Public Service Commission and, as such, those Regulations have been lawfully made; that the Committee constituted for the purpose of promotions is to determine the merit and suitability of the officers for promotion to the rank of Deputy Secretary on the basis of guideline given by the Government and prevailing practices in this regard; that there has been no arbitrary exercise of powers as all eligible candidates were given equal opportunity; that the petitioner availed himself of the promotion process and did not raise any objection on it at that time; but as he was not found fit he could not be promoted; that it is not correct that the petitioner has no alternative effective and equally efficacious remedy other than Writ Petition inasmuch as he has remedy in the Administrative Tribunal created under Act VII of 1981; that the fixation of seniority of officers of different Ministries had been done after consultation with the Ministry of Establishment and the Public Service Commission; that as the promotions were considered on the basis of merit, the petitioner and all other eligible officers including his juniors mentioned in the application and his seniors were considered for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary; that there was no examination held for the purpose of promotion to the rank of Deputy Secretary and, in fact, the Superior Selection Board made an evaluation of the candidates on the basis of their Annual Confidential Reports and other service recommendations and thereafter the Committee for Promotion held an interview to determine the overall suitability of the candidates for promotion to the rank of Deputy Secretary and in such due process of selection all candidates were given equal treatment and there was no scope for nepotism and corruption; that in the process of selection 60% marks were allocated for ACR and 40% marks for interview and since this was a case of promoting Class-I Officers to higher level of Class I posts consultation with the Public Service Commission was not necessary; that it is provided at serial No. 23 and 74(D) of the Schedule III of the Rules of Business, 1975, that specific Orders of the President are necessary for appointment to the post of Deputy Secretary and above and Regulation 3(b) of the Public Service Commission (Consultations) Regulations, 1979 provides that for appointment to the post requiring the specific order of the President, consultation with the Bangladesh Public Service Commission is not necessary and, as such, the Commission was not consulted; that it is not correct that the Superior Selection Board recommended the case of the petitioner for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary but the said Board submitted the eligible cases before the Promotion Committee for consideration of promotion to the rank of Deputy Secretary and the Promotion Committee recommended the cases for promotion; that the allegations and complaints against this system was baseless and newspaper reports on the matter are not based on actual facts nor the deliberations in the Parliamentary Standing Committee indicated any irregularity or illegality in this regard; that the Superior Selection Board did not recommend the petitioner or any other officer for promotion but the said Board simply submitted the cases of eligible candidates to the Committee for promotion to the rank of Deputy Secretary; that there has been no discrimination of the petitioner as an officer of 1973 batch of Civil Service nor the party in power treated the officers of 1973 batch as supporters of the Awami League nor the officers of 1977 batch are supporters of BNP; that the promotions of the officers to the rank of Deputy Secretary was not a political one but, an administrative decision for promotion on the basis of merit and suitability. 

 10. The petitioner filed an affidavit-in-reply to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 1 wherein he reiterated his statements made in the application and further stated that the Committee constituted under the notification dated 4.12.91 for the purpose or making appointment by promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary is not permissible as per Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitments Rules, 1981 that Superior Selection Board is the competent authority to recommend the person for appointment by promotion to the Post of Deputy Secretary in accordance with the Recruitment Rules and accordingly, the petitioner along with 373 superseded of his batch were recommended by the Superior Selection Board for appointment by promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary; that the Public Service Commission has been empowered under Article 140 of the Constitution to conduct test and examination for selection of the suitable persons for appointment in the service of the Republic and for making appointment by promotion to the higher post and to scrutinize the eligibility of the candidates; that Parliament may by law regulated conditions of service of the Republic as per, Article 133 of the Constitution and the President can also make Rule until provision in this behalf is made by any law; that Rule 5 of Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981 providing for Council Committee for Promotion, Superior Selection Board and Special Promotion Committee is not consistent with Article 140 of the Constitution and, as such, the said Rule is void according to Article 7(2) of the Constitution; that the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultation) Regulation 1979 have curtailed the Constitutional power conferred upon the Commission providing in Regulation No. 8, that it shall not be necessary to consult the Commission in cases of promotion within the same class of service; that this Regulation is in contravention of Constitutional provision of Article 140(2)(b) and, as such, void as per Article 7(2) of the Constitution; that the Committee formed under Annexure-A for holding test or interview for promotion for the post of Deputy Secretary has no power to do so since those powers have been vested with the Superior Selection Board as per BCS Recruitment Rules, 1981 and those powers were not given to any Committee by any Rules and the impugned Committee had no power to scrutinize the eligibility of the petitioner for the purpose of promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary when the Superior Selection Board found the petitioner fit for promotion; that since Administrative Tribunal cannot strike down any law or Rule on the ground of its constitutionality the petitioner is competent to seek remedy under Article 102(1) of the Constitution for enforcement of his fundamental right and for challenging vires of law; that Rules of Business, 1975 are not above the Constitution and provision made in serial No. 23 and 74(d) of Schedule III of the Rules of Business about the cases to be referred) to the President but the President should consult the Commission with respect to the principle to be followed in making appointment to the service of the Republic and promotion and transfer to service and suitability of the candidates for such promotion and transfer as per Article 140(2) (b) of the Constitution. By a supplementary affidavit filed on behalf of the respondent No. 1 it has been stated that the Council Committee took interview on the basis of guideline given by the Government; that interview and marking system was followed by the Council Committee in accordance with the guidelines and prevailing practices in order to assess the suitability of the officers to the rank of Deputy Secretary; that the Ministry of Establishment prepared a summary and submitted the same by Memo dated 3.11.91 containing the guidelines for promotion to the post of Deputy Secretary and Joint Secretary which were approved by the Cabinet as well as by the Prime Minister as the head of the Cabinet. 

 11. Writ Petition No. 813 of 1993 was filed by the petitioner, Md. Sarwar-e-Alam on 23.5.93 during the pendency of the Rules Nisi issued in the above mentioned two Writ Petitions and a Division Bench of this Court without issuing Rule directed the Writ Petition to be heard along with the aforesaid two Writ Petitions. In this application the petitioner also challenged the vires of Rule 5 of Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules 1981 providing for Council Committee on Promotion, Superior Selection Board and the Special Promotion Committee including the power to hold examination for appointment by promotion to the service of the Republic pursuant to notification dated 19.8.91 constituting Superior Selection Board and notification dated 10.10.91 constituting Council Committee; that petitioner also challenged the vires of the Bangladesh Civil Service Commission (Consultation) Regulations 1979 on similar grounds alleging, inter alia, that he obtained MSc Decree in Soil Science from Dhaka University in 1968 and appeared at the erstwhile EPCS Examination held in 1969 and was appointed as Section Officer and joined the said post on 8.12.70; that he was appointed Senior Scale Section Officer on 5.2.79 and was promoted to the post of Deputy Secretary on 30.7.85 like the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992. He appeared before the Council Committee on 11.12.91 in an interview for promotion to the post of Joint Secretary but the order of promotion issued on 8.2.92 did not include his name; that this petitioner also alleged supersession by his juniors as stated in the application and the grounds taken by him are similar to the grounds taken by the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992; and Mr. Shaheed Alam, the learned Advocate appearing on his behalf adopted the arguments of Mr. M Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992. 

 13. In Writ Petition No. 3193 of 1992 the same Division Bench issued a Rule Nisi on 18.10.92 on similar terms as in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992 with a direction for hearing both the Rules together. All the three matters were taken up for hearing by the Division Bench which by an order dated 18.11.93 referred the matter for hearing by a larger Bench as stated earlier. 

 15. As stated earlier the Rules were issued challenging the vires of Rule 5 of the Bangladesh Civil Service Recruitment Rules, 1981. The Rule is in the following terms: 

 17. The learned Attorney-General, however, on the other hand, has contended that the President need not consult the Public Service Commission on every matter and there are fields which are excluded from the purview of consultation. He has referred to Section 266 of the Government of India Act, 1935 wherein similar provisions were made for consultation with the Federal or Provincial Public Service Commission subject to the Regulations made by the Governor-General. In exercise of power given by the Government of India Act, 1935, the then Government of Bengal made the Bengal Public Service Regulations 1937 and Regulation 34 thereof provided that it shall not be necessary to consult the Commission with respect to the filling of certain posts. Article 320 of the Constitution of India provided in the proviso to Clause (3) thereof that the President 'as respects the all-India services and also as respects other services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union, and the Governor, as respects other services and post in connection with the .affairs of a State, may make regulation specifying the matters in which either generally, or in any particular class of case or in any particular circumstances, it shall not be necessary for a Public Service Commission to be consulted. Similarly Article 188 of the 1956 Constitution of Pakistan in Clause (2) therein provided that the President in respect of service and post in connection with the affairs of the Federation and the Governor of the Province in respect of service in connection with the affairs of the Province may make regulation in which it shall not be necessary for Public Service Commission to be consulted. Similarly, in the 1962 Constitution of Pakistan in Sub-Article (2) of Article 185 the President was authorized to provide by Order to dispense with Consultation with the Public Service Commission. 

 26. As to the formation of the Council Committee for Superior Appointment, Promotion and Service Structure rule 16 of the Rules of Business 1975 framed under Article 55(6) of the Constitution provides that the President of Council of Ministers may constitute standing Committee of the Council and assign necessary function to them and the composition and functions of such Committee may be amended or modified by the President. The first Council Committee was formed on the 6th of December, 1982; it was reconstituted on the 25th of July, 1983 and again the Council Committee was reconstituted by the impugned notification dated 10.10.91 (Annexure H in Writ Petition No. 2738 of 1992) wherein the Council Committee was composed of 7 Cabinet Ministers and one Minister of State with the Minister for Education as its convener. 

 27. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioners that the constitution of the Superior Selection Board and the Council Committee is ultra vires and in violation of the Constitutional provisions as contained in Part IX Chapters I and II of the Constitution inasmuch as these are in direct conflict with the Constitutional provisions and, as such, are liable to be declared illegal and void. As has been stated earlier the Superior Selection Board as well as the Council Committee were constituted in pursuance of the direction of the Government as notified from time to time, in exercise of the powers under rule 16 of the Rules of Business. No specific provision of the Constitution as mentioned in Chapters I and II of Part IX of the Constitution has been pointed out by the learned Advocate for the petitioner which is in conflict with the Superior Selection Board or Council Committee. The whole argument Of Mr. Islam is that any appointment or promotion in the service of the Republic must be done in consultation with the Public Service Commission but the learned Advocate has totally omitted the other provisions of law by which consultation with the Public Service Commission has been dispensed with. The argument of the petitioners under this head of challenge was that even if oral interview may be regarded in principle as a valid test for selection of candidates for admission to a college, it was in the present case arbitrary and unreasonable since the marks allocated for the oral interview were very much on the higher side as compared with the marks allocated for the written test. The marks allocated for the oral interview were 50 as against 100 allocated for the written test, so that the marks allocated for the oral interview came to 33-1/3% of the total number of marks taken into account for the purpose of making the selection. This, contended the petitioners, was beyond all reasonable proportion and rendered the selection of the candidates arbitrary and violative of the equality clause of the Constitution. Now there can be no doubt that, having regard to the drawbacks and deficiencies in the oral interview test and the conditions prevailing in the country, particularly when there is deterioration in moral values and corruption and nepotism are very much on the increase, allocation of a high percentage of marks for the oral interview as compared to the marks allocated for the written test cannot be accepted by the Court as free from the vice of arbitrariness. It may be pointed out that even in Peeriakaruppan’s: case (AIR 1971) SC 2303) (supra), where 75 marks out of a total of 275 marks were allocated for the oral interview, this Court observed that the marks allocated for interview were on the high side. This Court also observed in Miss Nishi Meghu's case (AIR 1980 SC 1975 (supra) "Reserving 50 marks for interview out of a total of 150 ........Does seem excessive, especially when the time spent was not more than 4 minutes on each candidate". There can be no doubt that allocating 3- 1/3 of the total marks for oral interview is plainly arbitrary and unreasonable. It is significant to note that even for selection of candidates for the Indian Administrative Service, the Indian Foreign Service and the Indian Police Service, where the personality of the candidate and his personal characteristics and traits are extremely relevant for the purpose of selection, the marks allocated for oral interview are 250 as against 1800 marks for the written examination, constituting only 12.2% of the total marks taken into consideration for the purpose of making the selection. We must therefore regard the allocation of as high a percentage as 33-1/3 of the total marks for the oral interview as infecting the admission procedure with the vice of arbitrariness and selection of candidates made on the basis of such admission procedure cannot be sustained. But we do not think we would be justified in the exercise of our discretion in setting aside the selection made for the academic year 1979-80 after the lapse of a period of about 18 months, since to do so would be to cause immense hardship to those students in whose case the validity of the selection cannot otherwise be questioned and who have nearly completed three semesters and, moreover, even if the petitioners are ultimately found to be deserving of selection on the application of the proper test, it would not be possible to restore them to the position as if they were admitted for academic year 1979-80, which has run out long since. It is true there is an allegation of mala fides against the Committee which interviewed the candidates and we may concede that if this allegation were established, we might have been inclined to interfere with the selections even after lapse of a period of 18 months, because the writ petitions were filed as early as October-November, 1979 and merely because the Court could not take up the hearing of the writ petitions for such a long time should be no ground for denying relief to the petitioners, if they are otherwise so entitled. But we do not think that on the material placed before us we can sustain the allegation of mala fides against the Committee. It is true, and this is a rather disturbing feature of the present cases, that a large number of successful candidates succeeded in obtaining admission to the college by virtue of very high marks obtained by them at the viva voce examination tilted the balance in their favour, though the marks secured by them at the qualifying examination were much less than those obtained by the petitioners and even in the written test, they had fared much worse than the petitioners. It is clear from the chart submitted to us on behalf of the petitioners that the marks awarded at the interview are by and large in inverse proportion to the marks obtained by the candidates at the qualifying examination and are also, in a large number of cases, not commensurate with the marks obtained in the written test. The chart does create a strong suspicion in our mind that the marks awarded at the viva voce examination might have been manipulated with a view to favouring the candidates who ultimately came to be selected, but suspicion cannot take the place of proof and we cannot hold the plea of mala fides to be established. We need more cogent material before we can hold that the Committee deliberately manipulated the marks at the viva voce examination with a view to favouring certain candidates as against the petitioners. We cannot, however, fail to mention that this is a matter which required to be looked into very carefully and not only the State Government but also the Central Government which is equally responsible for the proper running of the college, must take care to see that proper persons are appointed on the interviewing committee and there is no executive interference with their decision-making process. We may also caution the authorities that though, in the present case, for reasons which we have already given, we are not interfering with the selection for the academic year 1979-80, the selections made for the subsequent academic years would run the risk of invalidation if such a high percentage of marks is allocated for the oral interview. We are of the view that under the existing circumstances allocation of more than 15% of the total marks for the oral interview would be arbitrary and unreasonable and would be liable to be struck down as constitutionally invalid."
